extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians, and computer scientists interested in formal verification and the epistemology of proof
extracted.subtask_description: Characterizing what it is to 'understand' a mathematical proof by specifying the abilities, behaviors, and explanatory practices that constitute understanding; and relating those criteria to work in formal verification and automated reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness (formal verifiability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof must be correct in the sense that it can be modeled by formal axiomatic deduction; modern logic and formal axiomatic systems provide standards by which a proof is judged to be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic reduces correctness to pattern-matching against precisely specified rules; this is necessary but not sufficient for 'understanding'. Formal verification (proof assistants) can be used to check correctness rigorously. Note: correctness alone does not capture explanatory virtues or insights of a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to fill in details and justify inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to respond to challenges as to the correctness of the proof, and fill in details and justify inferences at a skeptic's request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes supplying missing steps that are omitted in textbook proofs; relevant for both pedagogy and formalization. Anti-pattern: accepting sketchy proofs without being able to justify omitted inferences when pressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to give a high-level outline/overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to give a high-level outline, or overview of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the main move(s), structure, and strategy without reproducing every low-level step. Useful for communicating the core idea and for pedagogical exposition. Anti-pattern: exposing only low-level calculations without conveying the overarching strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to recast the proof in different terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to cast the proof in different terms, e.g., eliminating or adding abstract terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate between formulations (concrete ↔ abstract) to show equivalences or expose different facets. Helpful for bridging communities and for implementation in different formal systems. Anti-pattern: proof tied rigidly to a single language or formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to identify key or novel points
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to pick out 'key' or novel points in the argument and separate them from steps that are 'straightforward'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out which lemmas/steps carry the conceptual weight versus routine deductions. This supports evaluation of originality and teaching focus. Anti-pattern: failing to distinguish novel insights from routine manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to motivate the proof (explain naturalness of steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to 'motivate' the proof, i.e., to explain why certain steps are natural or to be expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the guiding ideas and why particular choices are made; relating to Poincaré/Wittgenstein notions of discovery. This includes showing how steps could have been anticipated. Anti-pattern: presenting steps as arbitrary or 'capricious' without motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to provide natural examples and illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to give natural examples of the various phenomena described in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples and diagrams to illustrate the phenomena and make abstract points concrete. Helpful in teaching and in validating that constructions behave as claimed. Anti-pattern: purely formal presentation with no illustrative instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to indicate where hypotheses are needed and provide counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to indicate where in the proof certain of the theorem's hypotheses are needed, and to provide counterexamples that show what goes wrong if hypotheses are omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze dependence on assumptions; demonstrate necessity via counterexamples. This clarifies the scope of the theorem and deepens understanding. Anti-pattern: asserting hypotheses without showing their roles or necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to relate the proof to parallel developments or known proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to view the proof in terms of a parallel development, for example, as a generalization or adaptation of a well-known proof of a simpler theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the new proof onto familiar patterns to reveal its conceptual lineage and transferable methods. This aids discovery and transfer of techniques. Anti-pattern: treating the proof as isolated with no connections to existing methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to propose generalizations and weakenings
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to offer generalizations, or to suggest an interesting weakening of the conclusion that can be obtained with corresponding weakening of the hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify directions for extension and tradeoffs between hypotheses and conclusions. Important for research progress and for showing conceptual reach. Anti-pattern: failing to see or articulate natural generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to produce explicit constructions or calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to calculate a particular quantity, or to provide an explicit description of an object whose existence is guaranteed by the theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a theorem is non-constructive, show how to extract constructive content when possible; give explicit witnesses or algorithms. Anti-pattern: treating existence claims purely abstractly when explicit constructions are feasible and illuminating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to provide and justify diagrammatic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to provide a diagram representing some of the data in the proof, or to relate the proof to a particular diagram, and to justify diagram-based inferences despite representational choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand which diagrammatic features are essential and which are artifacts of a particular representation; justify inferences that generalize beyond the specific diagram (avoid illicit case-dependence). The Euclid example highlights the need to justify conclusions drawn from a particular diagram without exhaustive case-splitting. Anti-pattern: relying on a specific diagram to justify a general claim without showing why representational choices don't affect the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to manage domain embeddings and mixed numeric structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to reason correctly about numeric substructures (naturals, integers, rationals, reals, complexes), track embeddings/coercions, and ensure expressions are typed/qualified appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which domain an object belongs to (e.g., casting naturals to reals) and ensure orderings and operations are applied in appropriate domains. Important for formalization and avoiding subtle implicit assumptions. Anti-pattern: sloppy mixing of domains without explicit coercions or qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to formalize informal proofs in proof assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to translate informal, higher-level proofs into formal 'proof scripts' that make implicit inferences explicit so that proof assistants (Coq, Isabelle, ACL2, etc.) can verify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate the tedium of formalization (many routine inferences must be spelled out); use tactics, locales, coercions, and libraries to manage boilerplate. Recognize that formalization exposes hidden assumptions and that work in proof assistant design can reduce friction. Anti-pattern: assuming informal plausibility implies easy formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to manage proof search and automated reasoning heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to guide or design proof-search procedures: employ Skolemization, unification, cooperating decision procedures, heuristics to avoid combinatorial explosion (case-splitting), and exploit problem structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strategies that reduce search space (structure-aware methods, combining decision procedures, abstraction). Be wary of naïve case splits that cause combinatorial blowup (as in some geometric formalisms). Anti-pattern: brute-force case-splitting without exploiting invariants or higher-level lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to identify and formalize the mechanisms behind observed behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the ability to posit mechanisms or abstract abilities (recognize structures, apply lemmas, recall facts) that explain observable behaviors associated with understanding, and to use such models to teach or implement skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a functionalist/ability-based framework: articulate interacting abilities (some behavioral, some abstract) that explain understanding and can be targets for pedagogy or software models. Anti-pattern: treating understanding as an unanalyzable 'state' without specifying the operative abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expository and pedagogical clarity (useful definitions and presentations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce expository choices (natural definitions, fruitful generalizations, appropriate measurement of convenience) that guide inquiry and make proofs accessible and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose concepts and presentations that make calculations tractable and direct attention to fruitful directions (Wittgenstein's 'concepts lead us to make investigations'). Anti-pattern: choosing cumbersome definitions or presentations that obscure methods or make routine computations impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to explain the discovery process (logic of discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the capacity to explain how a proof or idea could have been discovered—discernment in selecting useful combinations and anticipating the train of inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate heuristic and methodological steps that would lead a competent mathematician to the proof (not merely justify it after the fact). This helps link understanding with creativity and pedagogy. Anti-pattern: offering only post-hoc justifications without illuminating the discovery heuristics.
